hints: Count the carbon chain in W from the skeletal formula in Fig. 5.1 and locate the position of the double bond to name W.
Think where else the same C=C bond could be placed on the same 7-carbon chain to make a different positional isomer, and which position still allows two different groups on each C=C carbon.
walkthrough:
Read what W really is**
Look at Fig. 5.1 together. Each end and each bend in a skeletal formula is a carbon. Counting along gives 7 carbons with the double bond starting at carbon 2, so W is hept-2-ene, $\text{CH}_{3}\text{CH}=\text{CHCH}_{2}\text{CH}_{2}\text{CH}_{2}\text{CH}_{3}$.

Move the functional group, not the chain**
A positional isomer keeps the same carbon skeleton and the same functional group, but the functional group moves. Here keep 7 carbons and one C=C, just change its position to 1-2 or 3-4. That gives hept-1-ene with $\text{C}=\text{C}$ at the end, and hept-3-ene with $\text{C}=\text{C}$ in the middle.

Draw both skeletally**
For hept-1-ene draw a 7-carbon zigzag with a double line at one end: $\text{C}1=\text{C}2$. For hept-3-ene draw a 7-carbon zigzag with the double line between C3 and C4. Either E or Z form of hept-3-ene is accepted here.

Final answer: Positional isomers: hept-1-ene, $\text{CH}_{2}=\text{CHCH}_{2}\text{CH}_{2}\text{CH}_{2}\text{CH}_{2}\text{CH}_{3}$ and hept-3-ene, $\text{CH}_{3}\text{CH}_{2}\text{CH}=\text{CHCH}_{2}\text{CH}_{2}\text{CH}_{3}$, both drawn as skeletal formulae with the C=C in the new position.

hints: Focus on what is special about the $\text{C}=\text{C}$ double bond compared with a $\text{C}-\text{C}$ single bond when groups try to swap sides.
walkthrough:
Picture the lock on the double bond**
A $\text{C}=\text{C}$ bond has a $\sigma$ bond plus a $\pi$ bond formed by sideways overlap of p orbitals. If you try to twist one end, you break that sideways overlap, so the twist does not happen at room temperature. The two ends are locked in place, and that lock is the origin of cis-trans (E/Z) stereoisomerism.
Final answer: Restricted / no rotation about the $\text{C}=\text{C}$ / $\pi$ bond.

hints: Compare the two atoms or groups attached to each carbon of the $\text{C}=\text{C}$ in W (hept-2-ene) with those in hept-1-ene.
walkthrough:
Apply the two different groups test**
Restricted rotation alone is not enough. You also need two different groups on the left C and two different groups on the right C. In W, hept-2-ene, C2 carries $\text{H}$ and $\text{CH}_{3}$, C3 carries $\text{H}$ and $\text{CH}_{2}\text{CH}_{2}\text{CH}_{2}\text{CH}_{3}$, so swapping gives a genuinely different arrangement in space. In hept-1-ene, C1 carries two $\text{H}$ atoms, so swapping them makes no difference and no stereoisomer exists.
Final answer: W has two different groups attached to each carbon of the $\text{C}=\text{C}$ bond, whereas hept-1-ene has two identical H atoms on C1 so shows no stereoisomerism.

hints: Keep the same connectivity as W (hept-2-ene) but place the two larger alkyl groups on opposite sides of the $\text{C}=\text{C}$ to the arrangement shown in Fig. 5.1.
walkthrough:
Flip one side of the double bond**
Stay with hept-2-ene, do not move the double bond. If Fig. 5.1 shows the two carbon chains on the same side (Z), draw them on opposite sides (E), and vice versa. The connectivity $\text{CH}_{3}\text{CH}=\text{CHCH}_{2}\text{CH}_{2}\text{CH}_{2}\text{CH}_{3}$ is identical, only the spatial arrangement across the rigid $\text{C}=\text{C}$ changes.

Final answer: Skeletal formula of the opposite E/Z isomer of hept-2-ene to that shown in Fig. 5.1, $\text{CH}_{3}\text{CH}=\text{CHCH}_{2}\text{CH}_{2}\text{CH}_{2}\text{CH}_{3}$ with alkyl groups transposed across the $\text{C}=\text{C}$.

hints: Look at the products, ethanoic acid and pentanoic acid, and think what has happened to the $\text{C}=\text{C}$ bond in terms of gain or loss of oxygen.
walkthrough:
Link bond breaking to oxygen gain**
The $\text{C}=\text{C}$ in W is completely broken and each carbon ends up in a $\text{C}=\text{O}$ of a carboxylic acid, $\text{CH}_{3}\text{COOH}$ and $\text{CH}_{3}\text{CH}_{2}\text{CH}_{2}\text{CH}_{2}\text{COOH}$. Gaining oxygen and losing electrons is oxidation, so X must be acting as the oxidising agent.

hints: Recall which strong oxidiser cleaves hot alkenes all the way to carboxylic acids rather than stopping at the diol or ketone stage.
walkthrough:
Choose the vigorous cleavage conditions**
Cold, dilute, alkaline $\text{KMnO}_{4}$ gives a diol, but to cut the chain right through to two acids you need vigorous conditions. That is hot and concentrated acidified $\text{KMnO}_{4}$, with heating, which oxidatively cleaves hept-2-ene at C2-C3 to give $\text{CH}_{3}\text{COOH}$ (2 carbons) plus $\text{CH}_{3}\text{CH}_{2}\text{CH}_{2}\text{CH}_{2}\text{COOH}$ (5 carbons).
